job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at seven in a shared flat in Edinburgh, with a flat white, and I'm at my desk by eight. I'm doing a master's in human-centred AI, and my days are lectures, a research assistant job two afternoons a week, and working on a scheduling tool I built with a friend. Last summer I interned at a small health-tech startup building a rota tool for district nurses. In the evening I go to a climbing session, or I cook with my flatmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right, honestly, and a bit of a relief for people who get anxious about it. At work I'd say the tools are useful but not magic. Online I'd probably post a thread about how to use them well, because I use them every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it still changes my day a bit, because I already use AI for code review and summaries. But it wouldn't take the job. I'd be quietly happy, since I'd be a person who already knows how to use them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the research assistant job and keep working on the nurse rota tool with my friend Meera. I'd also apply to about twenty companies that do human-centred design. And I'd try to get the tool in front of two local clinics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A steady world suits me. I do have about seventeen thousand in loans, and no offer yet, so I'm not totally relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've got no offer yet. How does that sit with feeling calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loans, mainly. I've got two months of savings and my mum, Karen, who's a physiotherapist, said she could cover a few months of rent. I'd rather not use it. I'd prefer to earn something from the rota tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the next year of graduates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it already doesn't feel like a revolution. It feels like a good set of tools. I'd tell the next batch of graduates to learn the basic tools in first year and then spend the rest of the time on real people's problems.

I'd post a thread online about how to use them **well**.
think: I already use AI for **code review** and summaries, so a plateau suits me.
I'm quietly happy to be someone who knows the tools **well**.
do: Finish the master's and keep the **research assistant** job.
Keep building the nurse **rota tool** with Meera.
Apply to about **twenty** human-centred design companies.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, with a small knot about loans and no offer yet.

Apply to about twenty human-centred design companies
Pitch the nurse rota tool to two local clinics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change work a lot, and we have to be careful about who it helps. I'd push for regulation of how companies use it on staff, and for workers to have a say. I'd also tell juniors to get hands on with the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the entry-level coding jobs are the first to feel it. My internship manager said she'd hire one junior instead of three. I'm good with the tools, so I think I'm on the right side of that, but it's competitive and I'm not sure I'm good enough to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in the human side, like designing tools nurses actually use, since that's what AI is bad at. I'd keep building the rota tool and try to turn it into a small paid pilot. And I'd apply for roles that mix design and engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. It's exciting, but I'd feel for people in my class who aren't adopting it. There's a part of me that's thrilled and a part that's thinking about my loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about in your class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the ones who say AI is a fad. They aren't getting practice, and in a year or two, the gap shows. I'd teach a short lunch session at the research lab, which feels more useful than arguing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a small success look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid pilot with a clinic, two or three thousand over a year, would cover my share of the rent. It's not a career, but it's a proof that I can sell something. Employers like seeing that.

I'd tell juniors to get **hands on** with the tools now.

I'm on the right side if I can **stand out**.
do: Specialise in **designing** tools nurses will actually use.
Turn the rota tool into a **paid pilot**.
Apply for roles mixing **design and engineering**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**: thrilled by the tools and thinking about loans.

fieldNote: Elena sees AI as both **opportunity and threat**, and tries to ride it.
She worries about **peers** who aren't adopting the tools.
Her answer is a **concrete pilot**, not a slogan.

steps.text: Teach a lunchtime session on AI tools at the research lab
Run a paid pilot of the rota tool with a clinic
Apply for roles mixing design and engineering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to move now, because two years is no time to retrain a country. I'd want a public discussion about income guarantees and who owns the systems. I'd also say it's exciting, which isn't a popular thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be nervous, because the graduate jobs I applied for would be gone before I'd had one. I'd still be better placed than most, because I know the tools, but better placed isn't safe. The one thing that might hold is work where a person must be present, like clinics and care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the rota tool toward clinics and care, which have patients and rules that slow down automation. I'd cut my rent by moving to my mum's flat in Glasgow, and put everything into savings. I'd take any job that would pay in the first six months, even a short contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and awake at three a.m. But also awake with a plan. I know it sounds odd, but I'm more excited than most of my friends, and that's strange when I know it could wipe out my first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about you being excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm the daughter who looks for the opportunity in a fire. Mum's job is hands-on and she's pretty sure it's safe for a while. She'd worry about my rent, and she'd quietly send me money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap for robots come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three-year gap for robots matters a lot to my mum's sort of work. For me it's the opposite: my work is the part that goes first. So I'd want to be useful to places where people still need people.

say: I'd say two years is **no time** to retrain a country, and we need income guarantees.
I'd say it's **exciting**, which isn't popular to say.
think: The graduate jobs I applied for would be **gone** before I'd had one.
Better placed isn't **safe**, but care work may hold.
do: Push the rota tool toward **clinics and care**.
Move to my mum's flat in **Glasgow** and save.
Take any **short contract** that pays in the first six months.
feel: I feel **anxious and awake** at three a.m., but with a plan.
S2.quote: I'm more excited than most of my friends, and that's strange when I know it could wipe out my first job.
fieldNote: Elena's **adaptive** streak shows: fear and excitement together.
She aims for **care settings** where robots and rules are slow.
Her mum would quietly **send money**, a safety net she prefers not to use.

steps.text: Pitch the rota tool to clinics and care homes in the first year
Move into my mum's flat in Glasgow to stop paying rent
Put all spare pay into a savings account
Take any short contract that pays within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent window, if we use it. I'd want governments to start pilots of income support and training now. I'd say to people at work that this is the time to build good habits with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be twenty-nine when full AGI arrives, with about four years of work behind me, probably in care technology. I'd be ahead of where I am now. After that, I don't know, and I'd be honest about not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in health tech after the master's, perhaps at the startup where I interned. I'd keep the rota tool going as a side project, save a few hundred a month and spend part of my time learning how to audit AI systems, since that looks like a job that lasts. I'd probably also join a co-operative of tech workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. Hopeful, a little scared. Five years is long enough that I could plan, but short enough that I couldn't pretend it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest choice in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether to specialise in auditing or in care design. Honestly I'd talk to a few people already doing both, like my lecturer Dr Nwosu, who audits hospital software. My gut says care design, because I like talking to nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a deposit on a flat, which I'd have wanted to buy at thirty. I'd rather rent for longer and keep money flexible. It's not what my mum would advise, but she's from a generation where a house was safe.

I'd tell colleagues this is the time to build **good habits**.
think: I'd be twenty-nine with about **four years** of work behind me, probably in care technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous and we should use it to redesign education and work. I'd say the tools should be open and shared. And I'd say we need something like a shorter working week, because productivity will be huge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-four with a decade of experience in tools that are changing, which is an advantage. The risk is more about the world than me: the question is who keeps the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my career in health tech and care design, saving steadily, buying a small flat in my early thirties and putting a bit into index funds. I'd stay in unions and co-ops that fight for shared gains. And I'd probably retrain once, in my thirties, into something like audit or policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some excitement. A decade is a long time. I'd worry about the people who aren't adopting the tools and can't see that coming, but I think I'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin who is choosing a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum to keep her physiotherapy skills sharp and not worry. And I'd tell my younger cousin, who's choosing a degree, to pick something where people matter to the result. She's thinking about law, and I'd say think about care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What role would you play in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be the one in the family who explains it all. I already do that with my mum about the chat tools. If it's ten years, I could help her retire in good shape, rather than watching her struggle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the first job I trained for might not exist. What would help is public training money, an income floor and clinics willing to try tools built by people like me. I'd also like to hear honest warnings from companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm either a doomer or a fan, and I'm both. I think the tools are brilliant, and the question of who owns them is what keeps me up at night. If I've got a chance to shape something, I'll take it.

headlineQuote: I think the tools are brilliant, and the question of who owns them is what keeps me up at night.
portrait: Elena is a **24-year-old** human-centred AI master's student in Edinburgh, with a computer science degree and a nurse-scheduling internship.
She uses AI **every day** and is building a rota tool with a friend, Meera, that she hopes to sell.
Her progressive views make her focus on **ownership and regulation** as much as skills.
She owes about **seventeen thousand** and has a mum, Karen, who could help with rent.
Her mood stays **calm or uneasy** in most worlds and turns anxious only when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her first job might not exist before she'd had a chance to hold it.
whatWouldHelp: **Public training money**, an income floor and clinics willing to try tools built by people like her.
